item.title: Oil Markets Brace for Renewed Iran Fighting
item.description:
Oct 24th, 2026
Oil Markets Brace for Renewed Iran Fighting
Bloomberg Economics Chief Emerging Markets Economist Ziad Daoud tells Bloomberg This Weekend that the risk of renewed fighting between the US, Israel and Iran is rising, helping keep oil prices elevated even as energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz recover. Speaking with hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini, Daoud says the conflict could remain a long-term stalemate, with heightened shipping costs, depleted stockpiles and escalating regional tensions continuing to threaten global energy supplies.

Kenya has reported a second death from Ebola, a 65-year-old woman who was a close family member of the index case, while Uganda said it’s restricting transit for anyone with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of the Congo in an effort to halt the disease spreading.
The deceased person in Kenya had been the third confirmed case in the country and had been in quarantine when she developed symptoms on Oct. 13, the East African nation’s health ministry said in a statement.

The house built by fixed income is facing an overhaul. Barclays Plc is showing it can do more for clients than trade bonds and arrange debt deals.
Barclays’ equities traders pulled level with their fixed income counterparts in the third quarter, the first time they pulled off such a feat since the UK lender acquired Lehman Brothers’ North American investment bank in 2008. It’s clear that Barclays sees a better future with a surging equities arm.

Indonesia is reducing natural gas exports to neighboring Singapore as President Prabowo Subianto seeks to shore up domestic supply and strengthen energy security for Southeast Asia’s largest economy.
The head of SKK Migas, the government agency overseeing Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas industry, said Saturday that pipeline-gas deliveries to the city-state were being cut by about 31 million standard cubic feet per day to help bolster domestic energy generation.

item.title: Odd Lots: How to Run a Restaurant For Three Decades (Podcast)
item.description:
Odd Lots: How a Chicago Restaurant Has Stayed Open For Nearly Three Decades
Odd Lots
How a Chicago Restaurant Has Stayed Open For Nearly Three Decades Arrow Right
48:45
Richard Mott's first foray into hospitality was in the 1980s at the University of Chicago, where he started running a coffee shop in the basement of the business school when he was a grad student. By the time he graduated, he helped grow that single coffee shop into four locations across campus. He's a longtime Chicago-based restaurateur and his farm-to-table restaurant North Pond has been around since the late 1990s. Lately, he's expanded his business to include Spark Shared Kitchen, a catering facility and incubator for food entrepreneurs. He knows a lot about the practical economics of restaurants and hospitality at large, and in his decades-long career in the Chicago scene he's seen about everything. On our recent trip to Chicago, we sat down with Mott to talk about the ever-increasing price of food and labor, why diners are drinking less, and the expected and unexpected reasons that restaurants so often fail.

Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
Shares of Switzerland’s ultra-defensive big companies are a bright spot in a tumultuous period for European equity markets.
The Swiss Market Index, which tracks the country’s 20 largest and most liquid stocks, has risen 4.6% this month while its euro-area counterpart, the Euro Stoxx 50, has fallen 3.2%. That outperformance of almost eight percentage points is the most by the Swiss benchmark since March 2020, when investors sought shelter from the shocks of the Covid-19 pandemic.

A developer of a liquefied natural gas facility in Alaska received financing from Russia-based Novatek PJSC, an energy giant that is subject to US sanctions, the Financial Times reportedBloomberg Terminal
.
Novatek offered funding to Polar Train LNG’s venture and directed its operations before required approvals were secured from the US Treasury, the newspaper cited the developer’s ex-chief executive officer Joel Riddle as saying in an interview. Riddle resigned last month, followed by other executives, according to the FT and a separate interviewBloomberg Terminal
with the New York Times.

India’s market regulator has ordered options trader Avadhut Sathe and his trading academy to refund 5.46 billion rupees ($57.5 million) to course participants after finding they provided unregistered investment advice and research services under the guise of stock market education.
In its final order, the Securities and Exchange Board of India also barred Sathe and Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy Pvt. from accessing the securities market for at least two years and directed them to pay 678.7 million rupees in interest.

Singapore expanded its investigation into haze-creating fires in Indonesia that have blanketed the city-state in smog, requesting information from 10 locally registered companies.
The National Environment Agency sent notices seeking documents and details of land concessions in Indonesia owned by the firms, their fire-fighting and blaze prevention measures, and their relationship to other relevant companies, according to a Friday statement.

item.title: Andrew Brandt on MLB Salary Cap Fight as World Series Begins
item.description: Andrew Brandt says the Brewers and Rays reaching the World Series—despite ranking 19th and 26th in payroll, respectively—shows how strong management, scouting and player development can compete with high spending. He calls the matchup evidence for the players’ union that success is possible without a salary cap, while cautioning that owners may dismiss it as an unsustainable exception: smaller-market teams have little margin for error and can lose players to wealthier clubs in free agency. He speaks with Romaine Bostick on "The Close." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: How Valterra's Forging the Future of Platinum | Chief Financial Officer
item.description: Chief Financial Officers now play a critical role in shaping corporate strategy and positioning organizations to meet future challenges. This episode profiles Valterra Platinum CFO Sayurie Naidoo, who leads the world's largest company producing platinum group metals. One year after its demerger from Anglo American, the South African firm is looking ahead to develop new markets for PGMs as the adoption of battery electric vehicles threatens their primary area of demand. (Source: Bloomberg)
